title: Retro style Final Fantasy inspired RPG - 9h build, no code
author: sharkymcstevenson2
selftext:
Hi everyone,

Here's a new game I'm working on since finishing the first version of my D2 inspired ARPG last week. This has been a project natively built on my own Tesana platform, similar to the ARPG previously except this time I'm not using any external assets whatsoever, not even UI elements. 

\- City map, two shops and two small areas completed so far.  
\- NPC's with voice dialogue and quests, shopkeeper and quest giver  
\- 9 hour build time so far  
\- All made with natural language (no code written)  
\- All models are AI generated, including furniture  
\- Music AI generated

All done without leaving the platform

**Question:** is the retro effect a bit too much? I was trying to go for an old school look and feel, but I feel like I might have overdone it.

  
There were a lot of requests last week for a tutorial, which I'll hope to have done this week as well. 



Let me know your thoughts!

comments.author: eduo
comments.body:
I'm all for AI game development, but I keep seeing how not having spent time at all making it is being presented as a flex and it concerns me.

It may be that I use AI differently, but 9h is not even enough to come up with enough game ideas to build a single game. At least one that brings something new.

replies.author: Illustrious_Web_4208
replies.body: I get it. I maybe spend 9 hours just getting the plans down and starting architecture. But let's be real this is cool AF and innovative. All of these are new and I'd like to see how different people utilise AI in different ways

replies.author: eduo
replies.body:
Yeah. I wasn't complaining about the post itself. Just how many posts focus on time as a main metric and how often it is that some foundational questions are not even answered by the time people are presenting something. 

My concern is that AI makes it so easy to have something visually available that we're skipping over having a clear idea of how things work out. 

It's a bit like the issue Marvel movies had with "temp music". Placeholder music that would be used before the final score was agreed. That "temp music" was usually a bad choice but by using it to prototype the edit and final cut it ends up shaping the final product, and by the time you try to choose music you can't really use anything that doesn't fit the "temp music" you didn't realize was shaping your end product.

Focusing too much on delivering a quick visual does the same thing: It shapes the final product in ways that may be hard to go back from unless you start from scratch afterwards.

  
I'm not sure I'm explaining it. It's unrelated to how cool the things being made with AI are and more about how we redefine the way we tackle projects to ensure that we don't sacrifice what really matters in the project (which in a Game is the game itself, its mechanics and "hook", if any).

replies.author: Illustrious_Web_4208
replies.body:
No I get it. AI has helped reduced the barriers to entry to many things but end of the day product is product and market will respond to good and bad ones as it always has. Faster time to market is a good thing but meeting consumer expectations is another beast of its own.

My core questions are also how does AI help meet consumer expectations? Or is there a new market of AI-related consumers...?
